o: a need to use their beaks more often, which made them bigger and was passed to their offspring
a constant mixing of populations across the islands, which averaged out their beak traits over many generations
geographic isolation and natural selection favoring beaks suited to different food sources on each island
sudden mutations caused by volcanic activity on the islands, which created new beak shapes in a single generation
quiz.e: Isolated on different islands with different available food, finch populations were selected for different beak shapes suited to local resources.

quiz.q: An adaptation that helps an organism survive in a desert environment might NOT be helpful
o: in any environment, since adaptations are always universally beneficial
in a very different environment, such as a rainforest
quiz.e: Adaptations are suited to specific environments; a trait beneficial in a desert may be neutral or harmful in a rainforest.

quiz.q: Which statement about evolution and individual organisms is correct?
o: Evolution happens when an individual organism changes its traits to match its environment during its lifetime
Evolution is a gradual process driven by a species' need to improve, so organisms purposely develop helpful traits
Evolution occurs only when populations split into separate species, never within a single, continuous population
Evolution is a change in a population's inherited traits over many generations, not within one organism's lifetime
quiz.e: Evolution describes change at the population level over generations — an individual's genes do not change because of its own life experiences.

quiz.q: Comparative embryology as evidence for evolution refers to
o: comparing the skeletons of adult organisms across related species
observing similar patterns of embryonic development among related organisms
studying fossilized eggs and nests of extinct animals
comparing the diets of embryos across different species
quiz.e: Related organisms often show strikingly similar stages of embryonic development, suggesting shared ancestry.

quiz.q: Antibiotic resistance becoming more common in a bacterial population after repeated antibiotic exposure is an example of
o: genetic drift acting only on a small bacterial population by chance
a vestigial trait that no longer serves any function
comparative embryology showing shared ancestry between bacteria
natural selection favoring resistant individuals that survive and reproduce
quiz.e: Bacteria with resistance survive antibiotic exposure and reproduce, making resistance more common in the population — a direct example of natural selection.

quiz.q: Which best explains why variation within a population is essential for evolution by natural selection?
o: Variation has no role, since the environment alone causes the changes
Without variation, there would be no differing traits for the environment to select among
Variation matters only for asexual organisms, since they cannot mutate
Variation prevents selection because every individual would then survive equally
quiz.e: Natural selection requires that individuals differ in traits so that some variants are more favored by the environment than others.

quiz.q: Which is the best example of an adaptation?
o: Thick fur that helps an animal survive in cold climates
An animal losing its tail in an accident during its lifetime
A person learning to swim after taking lessons
A plant that grows taller after being watered daily
quiz.e: Adaptations are inherited traits that improve survival and reproduction in a particular environment.

quiz.q: Fossils found in younger layers of rock are usually:
quiz.e: Younger layers are generally on top and contain fossils more like modern organisms.

quiz.q: What causes genetic variation in a population that natural selection acts on?
quiz.e: New alleles arise by mutation, and sexual reproduction shuffles alleles into new combinations.

quiz.q: Which statement is true about the theory of evolution?
o: It is just a guess that has not been tested by scientists
It claims individuals change during their life to meet their needs
It says organisms try to become better so they can survive
It is supported by many lines of evidence such as fossils and DNA
quiz.e: A scientific theory is a well-supported explanation, and evolution is supported by fossils, anatomy, embryos and DNA.

quiz.q: Why are bacteria becoming resistant to antibiotics?
o: Bacteria decide to become resistant when antibiotics are present
Antibiotics make bacteria directly stronger by changing their genes
Resistant bacteria survive and reproduce more than others
Humans get used to the medicine so it works less well
quiz.e: This is natural selection: the medicine removes non-resistant bacteria and resistant ones pass on their genes.

quiz.q: Which pair of animals most likely shares the most recent common ancestor?
o: Two species that live in the same place
Two species with very similar DNA
Two species that eat the same food
quiz.e: More similar DNA sequences indicate a more recent common ancestor.

quiz.q: Sunlight, temperature, and soil pH are all examples of
quiz.e: Abiotic factors are non-living components of the environment, such as sunlight, temperature, and soil chemistry.

quiz.q: An organism's specific functional role in its ecosystem, including what it eats and how it interacts with others, is its
quiz.e: Niche describes an organism's role/job in the ecosystem; habitat is simply where it physically lives.

quiz.q: In a food chain, producers are always
o: autotrophs that form the base of the chain
consumers that eat other organisms at the base of the chain
decomposers that break down dead matter for the chain
predators found at the top of the chain
quiz.e: Producers (autotrophs, like plants) make their own food and form the foundational base of every food chain.

quiz.q: An organism that eats both plants and animals is called a(n)
quiz.e: Omnivores consume both producers (plants) and other consumers (animals).

quiz.q: Fungi and bacteria that break down dead organisms and recycle nutrients are classified as
quiz.e: Decomposers break down dead organic matter and waste, returning nutrients to the ecosystem for producers to reuse.

quiz.q: A food web differs from a food chain in that a food web
o: shows only one species and its single food source in an ecosystem
shows the many interconnected, overlapping feeding relationships in an ecosystem
applies only to aquatic ecosystems and never to land habitats
never includes decomposers or the recycling of nutrients
quiz.e: A food web captures the complexity of real ecosystems, where most organisms have multiple feeding relationships, unlike a single linear food chain.

quiz.q: According to the 10% rule, approximately what percentage of energy is transferred from one trophic level to the next?
quiz.e: Only about 10% of energy at one trophic level is available to the next level up; roughly 90% is lost, mostly as heat.

quiz.q: Why do energy pyramids typically support only 4–5 trophic levels?
o: Because so much energy is lost as heat at each level that not enough remains to support additional levels
Because predators at higher levels are too large to be supported by the plants and small animals at the bottom
Because carbon dioxide and nutrients become too scarce at each level to allow the growth of more organisms
Because most producers die off before they can be eaten, leaving only a few primary consumers to feed on
quiz.e: With ~90% of energy lost at each level, there is eventually too little energy remaining to sustainably support further trophic levels.

quiz.q: The maximum population size an ecosystem's resources can sustainably support is called the
quiz.e: Carrying capacity is the population size an environment can sustain long-term given its available resources.

quiz.q: If a deer population grows well beyond its ecosystem's carrying capacity, which is the most likely outcome?
o: The population will keep growing indefinitely since food becomes more plentiful
Resources become scarce, increasing starvation/disease/competition until the population declines
The carrying capacity will automatically rise to match the larger population
Nothing will change because the ecosystem adjusts to any population size
quiz.e: Exceeding carrying capacity leads to resource scarcity, causing limiting factors (starvation, disease, competition) to reduce the population back down.

quiz.q: Which is an example of a limiting factor for a population?
quiz.e: Food, water, disease, predators, and space are all limiting factors that can restrict population growth.

quiz.q: Introducing a non-native, invasive species into an ecosystem often
o: has no effect on native species because they share the same resources
helps native species by adding biodiversity and food sources
can outcompete native species that lack natural defenses against it
improves the ecosystem's stability because it adds new interactions
quiz.e: Invasive species often outcompete native organisms that have no evolved defenses against them, disrupting the ecosystem.

quiz.q: Bioaccumulation of a toxic pollutant as it moves up a food chain is a concern primarily caused by
o: decomposers breaking down toxins so they become less concentrated at higher levels
producers filtering out all toxins so none reach higher trophic levels
pollution building up in tissues and becoming more concentrated at higher trophic levels
the 10% rule removing toxins as energy is lost at each level
quiz.e: Pollutants can accumulate in tissues and become increasingly concentrated (biomagnified) as they move up the food chain to top predators.

quiz.q: Deforestation primarily threatens biodiversity by
o: increasing available habitat and giving species more space to live
destroying/fragmenting habitat that many species depend on
increasing the carrying capacity for all species in the area
having no impact on population sizes of the species living there
quiz.e: Removing forest habitat displaces and endangers species that depend on that ecosystem, reducing biodiversity.

quiz.q: Which best describes the relationship between a community and its abiotic environment that together form an ecosystem?
o: An ecosystem is only the living populations, with soil, water, and climate counted separately
An ecosystem is one population of a species together with its predators and parasites
An ecosystem includes the community of populations PLUS the physical, non-living environment
An ecosystem includes only producers and decomposers, excluding consumers and the physical environment
quiz.e: An ecosystem combines the biological community with the physical (abiotic) environment they interact with.

quiz.q: Which of the following represents a correct simplified food chain?
quiz.e: Energy flows from producer (grass) to primary consumer (rabbit) to secondary consumer (fox).

quiz.q: What is the source of energy for most ecosystems?
quiz.e: Producers capture sunlight and make food energy for the rest of the food web.

quiz.q: What does a decomposer do in an ecosystem?
o: Makes its own food from sunlight and releases oxygen to the air
Breaks down dead matter and returns nutrients to the soil
Eats only plants and returns nutrients through its waste
Produces oxygen and carbohydrates for the rest of the ecosystem
quiz.e: Decomposers, such as fungi and bacteria, recycle nutrients.

quiz.q: If a food chain starts with grass, which organism is a secondary consumer?
o: A rabbit that eats grass and is eaten by a hawk
A mouse that eats grass and is eaten by a snake
A snake that eats a mouse that ate grass
A hawk that eats a snake that ate a mouse
quiz.e: The mouse is the primary consumer, so the snake eating the mouse is a secondary consumer.

quiz.q: Which action most helps conserve biodiversity?
quiz.e: Protecting habitat keeps species and their interactions intact.

quiz.q: The carbon cycle is balanced when carbon released by respiration and burning is:
o: Destroyed completely so that it leaves the cycle for good
Taken up again by photosynthesis and oceans
Stored only in the air as carbon dioxide gas
Turned into oxygen by the oceans and soil bacteria
quiz.e: Photosynthesis and the oceans remove carbon dioxide from the air, balancing release.

quiz.q: What happens to a population when it exceeds the carrying capacity?
o: It usually declines due to limited resources
It keeps growing forever because resources adjust to demand
It stays exactly the same because birth and death rates match
It stops needing food because it has adapted to the shortage
quiz.e: Resources run out, so death rates rise or birth rates fall until the population drops.

quiz.q: Homeostasis refers to an organism's ability to
o: grow larger over time as it takes in nutrients
maintain a stable internal environment despite external changes
reproduce sexually to pass genes to its offspring
evolve within a single generation to match its environment
quiz.e: Homeostasis is the maintenance of stable internal conditions (temperature, pH, water balance) regardless of external changes.

quiz.q: Sweating to cool the body down when its temperature rises is an example of
quiz.e: Negative feedback reverses a change (rising temperature) to restore the normal set point — this is the most common regulatory mechanism.

quiz.q: Which feedback mechanism intensifies a change rather than reversing it, such as during childbirth contractions?
quiz.e: Positive feedback amplifies a change and is used for processes with a clear endpoint, unlike the more common negative feedback.

quiz.q: In the circulatory system, blood vessels that carry blood AWAY from the heart are called
quiz.e: Arteries carry blood away from the heart; veins carry it back toward the heart.

quiz.q: Gas exchange between the lungs and blood occurs specifically in the
quiz.e: Alveoli are tiny air sacs where oxygen diffuses into blood and carbon dioxide diffuses out to be exhaled.

quiz.q: Hemoglobin, found in red blood cells, primarily functions to
o: digest food in the small intestine using enzymes
produce antibodies that fight pathogens in the blood
bind to and transport oxygen throughout the body
filter waste from the blood and form urine
quiz.e: Hemoglobin is a protein that binds oxygen in the lungs and carries it to tissues throughout the body.

quiz.q: Which organ is the main site of both chemical digestion and nutrient absorption?
quiz.e: The small intestine, aided by enzymes from the pancreas and bile from the liver, is where most digestion and absorption occur.

quiz.q: Villi in the small intestine function to
o: produce stomach acid to break down proteins in food
store undigested waste before it leaves the body
break down starch into sugars in the mouth
increase surface area for efficient nutrient absorption
quiz.e: The many finger-like villi greatly increase the surface area available for absorbing nutrients into the bloodstream.

quiz.q: Although the liver and pancreas assist in digestion, food does NOT pass directly through them because they are
o: not part of the digestive system at all, since they only filter blood
part of the respiratory system that supports gas exchange
accessory organs that produce digestive substances like bile and enzymes
involved only in excretion and the removal of nitrogenous waste
quiz.e: The liver and pancreas are accessory digestive organs — they contribute substances (bile, enzymes) but food does not physically travel through them.

quiz.q: A neuron transmits signals to the next neuron across a small gap called a
quiz.e: A synapse is the junction between neurons where chemical neurotransmitters carry the signal from one neuron to the next.

quiz.q: Which system uses antibodies and white blood cells to defend the body against pathogens?
quiz.e: The immune system defends against disease-causing pathogens using white blood cells and antibodies.

quiz.q: Vaccination works by
o: giving the body antibiotics that kill the pathogen directly, so the infection cannot take hold in the future
passing antibodies from another person's blood into the body, which provides temporary protection against disease
stimulating the body to produce heat and fever in advance, which prevents the pathogen from multiplying later
exposing the immune system to a weakened/inactive pathogen so it can 'remember' how to fight it later
quiz.e: Vaccines train the immune system to recognize and quickly respond to a specific pathogen in the future by producing antibodies in advance.

quiz.q: The kidneys' main function in the excretory system is to
o: digest fats and proteins using enzymes released into the small intestine
produce hormones only and have no role in filtering the blood
filter nitrogenous waste and excess water/salts from the blood, forming urine
exchange oxygen and carbon dioxide between the blood and the air
quiz.e: Kidneys filter blood to remove urea and excess water/salts, producing urine and helping maintain homeostasis.

quiz.q: The pancreas releasing insulin to lower blood glucose levels is an example of
o: the endocrine system regulating the body via a hormone in a negative feedback loop
the nervous system acting alone through fast electrical impulses in neurons
positive feedback with no endpoint that raises blood glucose even further
a structural adaptation that changes the shape of the pancreas over time
quiz.e: Insulin is a hormone (endocrine system) that signals cells to absorb glucose, lowering blood sugar — a classic negative feedback example.

quiz.q: Compared to the nervous system, hormone signals from the endocrine system typically
o: act more slowly but often have longer-lasting effects
act faster than nerve impulses and have shorter-lasting effects
have no real effect on the body unless nerve impulses are present
regulate only digestion and have no effect on growth or metabolism
quiz.e: Hormones travel through the bloodstream and generally act more slowly than electrical nerve impulses, but their effects often last longer.

quiz.q: Which best describes why organ systems must work together rather than in isolation?
o: They don't actually interact, since each system works independently
Homeostasis for the whole organism depends on coordinated function among multiple organ systems
Only one organ system is needed for survival, so the others are optional
Organ systems compete against each other for limited resources in the body
quiz.e: Maintaining homeostasis requires organ systems (circulatory, respiratory, nervous, endocrine, etc.) to work together in a coordinated way.

quiz.q: Which system transports nutrients and oxygen around the body?
quiz.e: The heart pumps blood through vessels to deliver oxygen and nutrients.

quiz.q: Which part of the brain controls balance and coordination?
quiz.e: The cerebellum coordinates movement and balance.

quiz.q: What is the main role of white blood cells?
quiz.e: White blood cells are part of the immune system and defend against pathogens.

quiz.q: Which organ produces bile that helps digest fats?
quiz.e: The liver makes bile, which is stored in the gallbladder and released into the small intestine.

quiz.q: Insulin and glucagon work together to:
quiz.e: Insulin lowers blood glucose and glucagon raises it, an example of negative feedback.

quiz.q: Which pathway does air take into the lungs?
quiz.e: Air passes through the nose, trachea and bronchi to the alveoli where gas exchange occurs.

PART_A.q: A student graphs the data from an experiment. The independent variable goes on the:

o: The number of seeds that germinate
The amount of water given to each seed

To make the independent variable larger

Ice contains more air than water
Ice has a lower mass than water molecules

o: Active transport uses energy to move substances against a gradient
Passive transport only moves large particles

Two species with very similar DNA

Humans get used to the medicine

o: Taken up again by photosynthesis and oceans
PART_A.e: Photosynthesis and the oceans remove carbon dioxide from the air, balancing release.

PART_A.q: Which action most helps conserve biodiversity?
PART_A.e: Protecting habitat keeps species and their interactions intact.

PART_A.q: Which pathway does air take into the lungs?
PART_A.e: Air passes through the nose, trachea and bronchi to the alveoli where gas exchange occurs.

PART_A.q: Insulin and glucagon work together to:
PART_A.e: Insulin lowers blood glucose and glucagon raises it, an example of negative feedback.

PART_A.q: Which organ produces bile that helps digest fats?
PART_A.e: The liver makes bile, which is stored in the gallbladder and released into the small intestine.

PART_B1.q: Which is the best example of a testable hypothesis?
o: Light is bad for some people
If plants get more light, then they will grow taller
PART_B1.e: A testable hypothesis makes a prediction that an experiment can support or reject, often in if-then form.

PART_B1.q: A scientist records that a plant grew 4 cm in one week. This is an example of:
PART_B1.e: Quantitative data are measurements with numbers and units. Qualitative data describe qualities such as color.

PART_B1.q: A plant bending toward a window to get more sunlight demonstrates the characteristic of life known as
PART_B1.e: Responding to an environmental stimulus (light) by growing toward it is a response to stimuli.

PART_B1.q: Which elements are always found in proteins?
PART_B1.e: Proteins are made of amino acids that contain carbon, hydrogen, oxygen and nitrogen, and sometimes sulfur.

PART_B1.q: What is the main function of carbohydrates in living things?
PART_B1.e: Carbohydrates, especially glucose, are the main quick source of energy for cells.

PART_B1.q: Which best explains why enzymes are considered reusable?
o: They are broken down after each reaction
They are not chemically changed or consumed by the reaction they catalyze
They only catalyze one reaction ever, then are discarded
They become part of the product
PART_B1.e: Enzymes speed up reactions without being permanently altered, so the same enzyme molecule can catalyze many reactions repeatedly.

PART_B1.q: Which organelle makes proteins?
PART_B1.e: Ribosomes build proteins from amino acids using instructions from mRNA.

PART_B1.q: Which organelle contains the cell's DNA in a eukaryotic cell?
PART_B1.e: The nucleus stores DNA and controls cell activities.

PART_B1.q: Which are the reactants of photosynthesis?
PART_B1.e: Plants use carbon dioxide and water, plus light energy, to make glucose and oxygen.

PART_B1.q: Which organelle captures light energy in a plant cell?
PART_B1.e: Chloroplasts contain chlorophyll, which absorbs light for photosynthesis.

PART_B1.q: What are the base pairing rules in DNA?
o: A with G and C with T
A with C and T with G
A with U and C with G
A with T and C with G
PART_B1.e: Adenine pairs with thymine and cytosine pairs with guanine.

PART_B1.q: If a plant with genotype TT is crossed with tt, what is the genotype of all offspring?
PART_B1.e: Each parent gives one allele, so every offspring gets T from one parent and t from the other.

PART_B1.q: Fossils found in younger layers of rock are usually:
PART_B1.e: Younger layers are generally on top and contain fossils more like modern organisms.

PART_B1.q: Which is the best example of an adaptation?
o: Thick fur that helps an animal survive in cold climates
An animal losing a tail in an accident
A plant that is watered daily
PART_B1.e: Adaptations are inherited traits that improve survival and reproduction in a particular environment.

PART_B1.q: If a food chain starts with grass, which organism is a secondary consumer?
o: A snake that eats a mouse that ate grass
PART_B1.e: The mouse is the primary consumer, so the snake eating the mouse is a secondary consumer.

PART_B1.q: What does a decomposer do in an ecosystem?
o: Breaks down dead matter and returns nutrients to the soil
PART_B1.e: Decomposers, such as fungi and bacteria, recycle nutrients.

PART_B1.q: What is the source of energy for most ecosystems?
PART_B1.e: Producers capture sunlight and make food energy for the rest of the food web.

PART_B1.q: What is the main role of white blood cells?
PART_B1.e: White blood cells are part of the immune system and defend against pathogens.

PART_B1.q: Which part of the brain controls balance and coordination?
PART_B1.e: The cerebellum coordinates movement and balance.

PART_B1.q: Which system transports nutrients and oxygen around the body?
PART_B1.e: The heart pumps blood through vessels to deliver oxygen and nutrients.

PART_B2.q: Which best describes reproduction as a characteristic of life?
o: Organisms produce offspring, either asexually or sexually
Reproduction always produces genetically identical offspring
PART_B2.e: Reproduction can occur asexually (one parent, identical offspring) or sexually (two parents, genetic variation).

PART_B2.q: A nucleotide is made of which three components?
o: An amino acid, a fatty acid, and a phosphate
A sugar, a phosphate group, and a nitrogenous base
A protein, a lipid, and water
PART_B2.e: Each nucleotide consists of a sugar, a phosphate group, and one nitrogenous base.

PART_B2.q: A cell placed in an isotonic solution will
o: show no net change in water movement
PART_B2.e: In an isotonic solution, solute concentrations inside and outside are equal, so there is no net movement of water.

PART_B2.q: Which phase of the cell cycle involves DNA replication before mitosis begins?
PART_B2.e: Interphase is when the cell grows, carries out its normal functions, and replicates its DNA before dividing.

PART_B2.q: Both autotrophs and heterotrophs carry out
o: cellular respiration to release energy from glucose
PART_B2.e: All organisms, whether they make their own food or consume it, perform cellular respiration to release usable energy from glucose.

PART_B2.q: Which gas is released as a waste product of the light-dependent reactions of photosynthesis?
PART_B2.e: Water is split during the light-dependent reactions, releasing oxygen as a byproduct.

PART_B2.q: Which structure is a tightly coiled/condensed form of DNA wrapped around proteins?
PART_B2.e: A chromosome is DNA condensed and organized around proteins so it can be reliably copied and separated during cell division.

PART_B2.q: Which best explains why variation within a population is essential for evolution by natural selection?
o: Variation has no role in evolution
Without variation, there would be no differing traits for the environment to select among
Variation only matters for asexual organisms
Variation prevents natural selection from occurring
PART_B2.e: Natural selection requires that individuals differ in traits so that some variants are more favored by the environment than others.

PART_B2.q: Which of the following represents a correct simplified food chain?
PART_B2.e: Energy flows from producer (grass) to primary consumer (rabbit) to secondary consumer (fox).

PART_B2.q: Which best describes why organ systems must work together rather than in isolation?
o: They don't actually interact with each other
Homeostasis for the whole organism depends on coordinated function among multiple organ systems
Only one organ system is needed for survival
Organ systems compete against each other for resources
PART_B2.e: Maintaining homeostasis requires organ systems (circulatory, respiratory, nervous, endocrine, etc.) to work together in a coordinated way.

PART_C.q: Written response: choose TWO concepts from different units and construct an argument connecting them. Cite specific evidence from each.
o: Names both concepts precisely, gives concrete evidence for each, and explains the causal/logical bridge
Lists the two topics without connecting them
Describes only one concept in detail
Gives a personal opinion with no course evidence
PART_C.e: Strong responses anchor every claim in specific unit content.

PART_C.q: Essay plan: identify the single most important takeaway of this course. Defend it using three units as evidence, then address one counterargument.
o: Clear thesis, three unit-specific pieces of evidence, genuine counterargument, resolution
PART_C.e: Full argumentative architecture earns top marks.
